---
title: "Prediction bias and prediction variance"
---

The earlier pages defined [estimator bias](../statistical-inference/estimator-bias.qmd), [estimator variance](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd), and their contribution to [mean squared error](../statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd). Here the estimator is a fitted prediction at a specified predictor value. The same decomposition thus concerns prediction bias and prediction variance across repeated training samples.

Suppose we use lexical frequency to predict first-fixation duration. Frequency effects are well established in eye-tracking studies, but a fixation duration remains an eye-movement measurement rather than a direct measurement of lexical access. A straight line may miss a real bend in the conditional association. A very flexible curve may instead follow accidental bumps in the particular sample used to fit it. Both procedures can make poor predictions, but they fail for different reasons.

The [**bias-variance decomposition**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) separates error that persists across repeated training samples from variation in the fitted prediction across those samples. It is useful because a model can reduce one source of error while increasing the other.

## Beginning with repeated training samples

Let $x$ be a particular predictor value, such as a log frequency of 4. For current purposes, $f(x)$ averages over the other properties of readers, words, and contexts represented by the data-generating process. It is not a claim that frequency alone causes the response. Suppose that the response for a fixated word position with that frequency is generated by

$$
Y=f(x)+\varepsilon,
$$

where $f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ is the true conditional mean and the noise term satisfies

$$
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X=x)=\sigma^2.
$$

Now imagine repeatedly drawing a comparable corpus and fitting the same complete analysis procedure to each corpus. The procedure produces a prediction $\widehat{f}(x)$ from every training sample. Thus, $\widehat{f}(x)$ is itself a random variable across training samples, even though any one fitted model returns a fixed number.

This repeated-sample interpretation is essential. Prediction variance does not describe variation among words with the same frequency. It describes variation among the predictions that would be learned from different training samples.

## Defining bias and prediction variance

The bias of the learning procedure at $x$ is

$$
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat{f}(x))
=
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]-f(x).
$$

The expectation averages the predictions across repeated training samples. If a straight line systematically predicts 20 ms too much at low-frequency words, its bias at that value is 20 ms.

The prediction variance at $x$ is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{f}(x))
=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\left(
\widehat{f}(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]
\right)^2
\right].
$$

A procedure has high prediction variance when small changes in the training corpus produce large changes in its fitted prediction. A highly flexible curve may have this property because each corpus contains different accidental bumps.

## Deriving the decomposition

We want the expected squared error for a new response $Y$ at the fixed value $x$. This response is generated independently of the training sample, conditional on $x$:

$$
\mathbb{E}
\left[
(Y-\widehat{f}(x))^2
\right].
$$

Add and subtract both $f(x)$ and $\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]$ inside the error:

$$
Y-\widehat{f}(x)
=
\underbrace{Y-f(x)}_{\text{response noise}}
+
\underbrace{f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]}_{\text{negative bias}}
+
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\widehat{f}(x)]-\widehat{f}(x)}_{\text{training-sample variation}}.
$$

Squaring this sum produces three squared terms and three cross-products. The expected cross-products are zero. The response noise has mean zero, and the fitted prediction is centered around its own expectation. We are left with

$$
\mathbb{E}
\left[
(Y-\widehat{f}(x))^2
\right]
=
\sigma^2
+
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat{f}(x))^2
+
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{f}(x)).
$$

The first term is the conditional response variance. In the bias-variance decomposition, it is often called [**irreducible error**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) because even a procedure that knows $f(x)$ exactly cannot predict which particular response noise will occur. The second and third terms arise from the learning procedure and may change when the model, fitting rule, or sample size changes.

## Working through one frequency value

Suppose procedure A fits a straight line. At one frequency value, repeated samples show a bias of 20 ms and a prediction standard deviation of 15 ms. Its reducible expected squared error is

$$
20^2+15^2
=
400+225
=
625\text{ ms}^2.
$$

Procedure B fits a more flexible curve. Its bias is only 5 ms, but its prediction standard deviation is 30 ms:

$$
5^2+30^2
=
25+900
=
925\text{ ms}^2.
$$

Procedure B is closer to the true mean on average, so it has lower bias. But a particular fit from procedure B is much less stable across corpora. At this predictor value, the larger variance more than offsets the smaller bias.

Suppose the irreducible error is $40^2=1600\text{ ms}^2$ for both procedures. Their complete expected squared errors are then 2225 and 2525. This term changes the total error but not the comparison, since both procedures predict the same response process at the same $x$.

## Representing the calculation in R

The hand calculation can be represented directly.

```{r}
#| eval: false

procedure <- data.frame(
  model = c("straight line", "flexible curve"),
  bias_ms = c(20, 5),
  prediction_sd_ms = c(15, 30)
)

procedure$bias_squared <- procedure$bias_ms^2
procedure$prediction_variance <- procedure$prediction_sd_ms^2
procedure$reducible_mse <-
  procedure$bias_squared + procedure$prediction_variance

procedure
```

The code does not estimate bias or variance from one corpus. It merely carries out the decomposition after those quantities have been supplied from a repeated-sampling argument, a simulation, or another justified source.

## Bias and variance across model classes

It is tempting to call simple models high bias and flexible models high variance. That slogan is sometimes useful, but it is not the definition. Bias and variance are properties of a complete learning procedure under a particular sequence of repeated samples.

Regularization may make a flexible curve stable. [Partial pooling](../regression-models/random-effects.qmd) may reduce variation in conditional predictions for sparsely observed verbs. A larger training sample may reduce the prediction variance of both procedures. Conversely, an unregularized model with only a few poorly identified parameters may be unstable.

Thus, coefficient count alone does not determine prediction variance. The sampling process, model, preprocessing, and fitting rule all matter.

## What one dataset cannot reveal

We observe only one corpus, not the repeated corpora in the definitions. Because the decomposition averages over hypothetical training samples, one observed dataset does not separately identify true bias and prediction variance.

Cross-validation can estimate their combined consequence for held-out prediction. Repeated cross-validation may also show that a model comparison is sensitive to the fold assignment. But neither procedure reveals the true bias term without additional assumptions about $f(x)$ or a simulation in which the data-generating process is known.

If a flexible model has worse held-out loss, we may say that its complete learning procedure predicts worse for the chosen prediction unit, information set, population, and loss. We should not claim that prediction variance caused the difference unless the design separately supports that diagnosis. And we should not promote a difference in predictive performance into an explanation of the linguistic process that generated the response.

## Checking the decomposition

1. Across what repetitions is $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{f}(x))$ defined?
2. In the numerical comparison, which procedure has lower bias and which has lower reducible expected squared error?
3. If procedure A and procedure B predict the same response process at the same $x$, why does irreducible error not affect which one has lower expected squared error?
4. Why can a flexible regularized model have lower prediction variance than a smaller unregularized model?
5. What can held-out loss establish that the separate bias and variance terms cannot be estimated to establish from one corpus?

The bias and variance decomposition explains why a procedure that follows the training data more closely need not predict new responses better. Prediction variance concerns new training samples, while irreducible error arises from new responses at a fixed predictor value. The [next page](training-and-test-data.qmd) turns this repeated-sample argument into an observable evaluation by separating fitting data from test data.
